StringWithMarkup.String: 2-Methyl-1,4-benzoquinone may be released in various waste streams during the extraction and refining of oil. If released to the atmosphere, 2-methyl-1,4-benzoquinone should exist mainly in the vapor phase based on an estimated vapor pressure of 3.4X10-2 mm Hg at 25 °C. Vapor-phase 2-methyl-1,4-benzoquinone is degraded in the atmosphere by reaction with photochemically produced hydroxyl radicals; the half-life for this reaction is estimated to be about 29.5 hours. In soil, 2-methyl-1,4-benzoquinone is expected to have high to very high mobility based on estimated Koc values of 2 and 60. Volatilization of 2-methyl-1,4-benzoquinone from dry soil surfaces is expected to be slow based upon its vapor pressure; this compound should not volatilize from moist soil surfaces based on an estimated Henry's Law constant of 1.9X10-9 atm-cu m/mole. 2-Methyl-1,4-benzoquinone may not be readily biodegraded as initial wastewater concentrations of 1-4 ng/g were unchanged in final effluents following activated sludge treatment. 2-Methyl-1,4-benzoquinone is not expected to adsorb to sediment and particulate matter in the water column, based on its Koc values, or to volatilize from water surfaces, based on its Henry's Law constant, or to bioconcentrate in aquatic organisms, based on an estimated BCF value of 2. Exposure to 2-methyl-1,4-benzoquinone may occur occupationally during the extraction and refining of oil. (SRC)

Section.Description: Sorption to soils and sediments is an important factor on the transport and fate of organic contaminants in the environment.  The soil/water adsorption coefficient, also known as solid-water distribution coefficient (Kd), measures the amount of chemical substance adsorbed onto soil per amount of water.  Since adsorption occurs predominantly by partition into the soil organic matter, it is more useful to normalize the Kd value to the organic carbon content of a soil and express the distribution coefficient in Koc (organic carbon normalized distribution coefficient).  The greater the Kd (or Koc) value, the less likely a chemical will leach or contribute to runoff.  A very high value means it is strongly adsorbed onto soil and organic matter and does not move throughout the soil.
